title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
author: Zheyuan (Kevin) Cui · Mert Demirer · Sonia Jaffe · Leon Musolff · Sida Peng · Tobias Salz

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied excerpt contains only bibliographic references and gives no findings, reasoning or recommendations from the source itself. Although some cited titles concern human–computer performance and field evidence on AI productivity and quality, they do not establish the source’s position on whether benchmark scores have real-world professional meaning or how benchmarks should be governed.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Provides material randomized workplace evidence from software development that AI assistance can raise output substantially while producing heterogeneous, uncertain gains across experience groups. This strengthens the cluster’s claims about bounded productivity and user-dependent benefits, though it does not directly test legal work, verification, competence formation or lawyer replacement.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Provides material field-experimental evidence from software development that strengthens the cluster’s claims about meaningful task-level gains, uneven effects and the gap between tool access and realised workplace value. It finds higher output but also substantial uncertainty, cross-company variation, incomplete adoption and suggestive heterogeneity favouring junior or less-productive users; it does not directly address legal verification or prescribe operating-model redesign.
qs: This suggests that factors other than access, such as individual preferences and perceived quality of the tool, play important roles in engineers’ decisions to use this tool (Dietvorst, Simmons, and Massey 2015, 2018).

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s outcome-specific treatment of productivity evidence: it finds a substantial increase in completed coding tasks, especially among less-experienced developers, while not measuring employment, income or durable learning and emphasizing uncertainty about broader productivity effects.

Uncertainty around firms’ willingness to adopt these technologies and their capacity to make necessary complementary investments (Bresnahan 2024; Brynjolfsson, Rock, and Syverson 2021) makes it currently difficult to empirically assess whether or not optimism about productivity gains is justified.1 Nevertheless, some applications of generative AI have already matured and are integrated into existing workflows.

st.t: Coding workflow: Generation overhead limits productivity gains
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by showing that Copilot’s productivity gains are uneven—significant for junior and recent hires but not statistically significant for senior or longer-tenured developers—and by warning that human review remains necessary to prevent errors or reduced code quality. Its randomized field evidence and methodological caveats reinforce the cluster’s distinction between faster task completion and reliable, generalizable productivity gains.
qs: We find that Copilot significantly raises task completion for more recent hires and those in more junior positions but not for develop- ers with longer tenure and in more senior positions.
If developers rely on it without review, it could potentially introduce errors or decrease code quality.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster by finding positive workplace output effects while limiting them to measured coding activity and warning that coding-task savings do not translate fully into whole-job productivity. It also treats quality risks as unresolved and provides no evidence that assisted output gains produce durable skill growth.
qs: Additionally, coding is only part of a software developer’s job, so only some of the time saved on coding tasks may be spent on addi- tional coding.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s conditional account by providing causal workplace evidence of sizable task-level output gains from an integrated coding assistant, while explicitly cautioning that adoption and complementary investment limit broader productivity conclusions. It does not determine whether weaker users gain more than stronger users.

kp.k: Randomized workplace experiments test AI-assisted software development
kp.d: The February 2025 manuscript, identified in the supplied heading as Management Science (2026), analyzes company-run randomized trials of GitHub Copilot at Microsoft, Accenture and an anonymous Fortune 100 electronics manufacturer. Experiments lasted 2–8 months before all groups received access. The analyzed sample comprises 4,867 developers: 1,521 at Microsoft, 316 at Accenture and 3,030 at Anonymous Company after exclusions. This is evidence about software development, not measured effects on legal work. The authors disclose that the RCT was post-registered and that implementation reflected business rather than research priorities.
qs: These experiments lasted 2 to 8 months after which all groups were granted access to Copilot.
This RCT was post-registered as AEARCTR-0014530 (Peng 2024).
The exact implementation of these experiments was rather ad-hoc as they were driven by business considerations at these companies rather than research goals.

kp.k: Copilot augments coding within developers’ existing tools
kp.d: The studied assistant generates code snippets, comments and documentation from surrounding code or plain-text instructions. Its proposed time-saving mechanisms are replacing manual typing and online searches, while potentially supplying useful suggestions developers would not otherwise identify. The authors explicitly warn that accepting suggestions without review can introduce errors; the intervention is code assistance rather than autonomous completion of developers’ entire jobs.
qs: As developers write software code or plain text comments, Copilot analyzes the context and generates relevant code snippets, comments, and documentation.
It can autocomplete code that developers might manually type or suggest snippets they would otherwise need to search for online.
If developers rely on it without review, it could potentially introduce errors or decrease code quality.

kp.k: Preferred estimate shows 26.08% more completed tasks
kp.d: The precision-weighted combination of experimental estimates finds a 26.08% increase in weekly pull requests, the study’s completed-task measure, with SE 10.3%. Secondary estimates are 13.55% more commits (SE 10.0%) and 38.38% more builds (SE 12.55%). Table 2 marks the pull-request and build estimates as statistically significant, but not commits. These are effects attributed to adoption using randomized access as an instrument, rather than an average effect of merely offering access to every developer.
qs: on average, the number of weekly pull requests made by developers increases by 26.08% (SE: 10.3%), the number of weekly commits increases by 13.55% (SE: 10.0%), and the number of weekly builds increases by 38.38% (SE: 12.55%).
Because of imperfect compliance, our preferred estimates use treatment status as an instrument for usage, so this is an estimate of the treatment on the treated.

kp.k: Workflow metrics measure output, not comprehensive work quality
kp.d: The primary outcome is pull requests, whose scope is shaped by organizational conventions and can differ between firms. Pull requests trigger code review before merging into a larger project. Commits and builds capture intermediate activity rather than deliverables, while build success is used as a code-quality proxy. Considerable variation and many zero-output developer-weeks constrain statistical power.
qs: A main outcome of interest is “pull requests”, which can be thought of as a unit of work for software developers.
A pull request will lead to a code review, often by a more senior software developer.
While commits and builds do not directly correspond to a deliverable, we expect them to be nevertheless monotone in the amount of accomplished work.
Lastly, we use the build success rate as a measure of code quality.

kp.k: Adoption remains incomplete despite access and workflow integration
kp.d: At Microsoft, only 8.5% of the treated group signed up during the first two weeks; reminders on February 15 and February 28, 2023 increased take-up to 42.5% within two weeks. Accenture paired access with training and manager encouragement, obtaining faster initial adoption that plateaued around 60% after 1–2 months. The authors report that around 30–40% of engineers never tried the product despite relatively easy adoption, suggesting that access alone does not determine uptake. Adoption is defined cumulatively and does not necessarily mean continued use.
qs: We define the adoption period as the first time a software engineer uses GitHub Copilot and consider an engineer as having adopted the tool even if they later stop using it.
These additional emails increased the take-up rate to 42.5% within two weeks of being sent.
Despite this, the adoption rate is significantly below 100% in all three experiments, with around 30-40% of the engineers not even trying the product.

kp.k: Weighted instrumental variables address imperfect compliance and convergence
kp.d: The preferred regressions instrument adoption with randomized assignment, controlling for developer and week fixed effects. Because control groups eventually gained access, adoption differences diminished and weakened the instrument. Weighting periods by treatment-control adoption differences improves precision; separate company estimates are then pooled by precision. The authors caution that weighting changes the targeted effect if treatment effects vary over calendar time. Appendix Table 3 reports an unweighted pooled pull-request estimate of 18.73% (SE 15.1%), compared with the preferred 26.08% (SE 10.3%).
qs: we weight the 2SLS estimates by the (period-by-period) difference in adoption across treatment and control groups.
If, on the other hand, treatment effects are unchanged over the course of the experiment, the weighting will purely improve the precision of our estimates without affecting their interpretation.

kp.k: Individual experiments yield uncertain and heterogeneous estimates
kp.d: Table 2 reports weighted-IV pull-request effects of 27.38% at Microsoft (SE 12.88%), 17.94% at Accenture (SE 18.72%) and 54.03% at Anonymous Company (SE 42.63%); only Microsoft’s individual estimate is marked statistically significant. The authors attribute limited power to highly variable output, initially low Microsoft adoption, the small Accenture sample and brief access differences during Anonymous Company’s staggered rollout. Observational difference-in-differences estimates can be either above or below experimental estimates.
qs: Interestingly, we find that our difference-in-difference estimates are sometimes larger and sometimes smaller than the experimental estimates, emphasizing that the reasons for the divergence between experimental and observational estimates may differ across companies.
At Accenture, only a few hundred developers participated in the experiment.
Lastly, at Anonymous Company, the treatment consisted of a staggered rollout with differences in treatment status lasting only a short time.

kp.k: More builds need not mean proportionately better work
kp.d: The authors consider whether increased builds reflect trial-and-error acceptance of AI suggestions followed by compilation checks rather than straightforward efficiency improvements. Table 2 reports a build-success effect of −1.34% at Microsoft (SE 4.23%), −17.40% at Accenture (SE 7.12%, statistically significant) and −5.53% pooled (SE 3.64%, not marked significant). They describe the trial-and-error interpretation as only weakly supported at Accenture and raise possible long-run quality deterioration as a concern, not an established finding.
qs: A less optimistic interpretation of the increase in builds is that developers may engage in more trial-and-error coding, accepting Copilot’s suggestions and then compiling the project to check for errors.
Such a change in coding style could lead to lower-quality code in the long run and undermine efficiency gains in the quantity of code.
However, our results on build success rate only (weakly) support such an interpretation for the Accenture experiment.

kp.k: Less experienced developers show higher adoption and gains
kp.d: Microsoft-only subgroup analyses find short-tenure developers 9.4 percentage points more likely to adopt (SE 2.2pp; 81.6% versus 72.1%) and junior developers 4.7 percentage points more likely (SE 2.2pp; 79.2% versus 74.4%). Preferred output estimates are larger for short-tenure developers (27–39% versus 8–13%) and juniors (21–40% versus 7–16%). However, the detailed results and Figure 6 qualify differences as noisy and typically not statistically significant. Short-tenure developers also persist in use more, potentially contributing to the estimated tenure gap.
qs: short-tenure developers increase their output by 27% to 39% while long-tenure developers have smaller gains of 8% to 13%.
For all three outcome measures, the effects on productivity are stronger for short-tenure/junior/less productive developers, though the difference is typically not statistically significant.
The estimates for above and below-median productivity developers are even noisier but directionally consistent.

kp.k: Lower prior productivity predicts greater suggestion acceptance
kp.d: At Microsoft, developers with lower pre-experiment productivity accept a significantly larger fraction of suggestions. Figure 5 reports 25.9% versus 24.2% for below- versus above-median pre-productivity, with p=0.01. This does not translate into clearly higher persistence: lower-productivity developers are, if anything, less likely to continue using Copilot, with p=.085. The authors therefore document distinct patterns for initial adoption, continued use and suggestion acceptance.
qs: developers who were less productive before the experiment are significantly more likely to accept any given suggestion.
Figure 4(c) shows that, if anything, low-productivity developers are less likely to continue using Copilot, though the difference is (just) not statistically significant (p=.085).

kp.k: Abandoned experiment weakens but does not reverse pooled gains
kp.d: An additional April 2023 Accenture experiment was abandoned after layoffs affected 42% of participants. Analysis of 204 remaining developers required imputing missing control-group adoption data. Its pull-request estimate is −39.18% (SE 36.78%), statistically insignificant. Including it reduces the pooled pull-request estimate to 21.34% (SE 9.92%); pooled commits and builds become 15.39% (SE 9.69%) and 37.03% (SE 12.22%). The authors disclose the negative result and data limitations; they do not attribute the layoffs to Copilot.
qs: In particular, we lack adoption data for the control group until October ’23. Without this adoption data, any analysis is potentially biased.
We find a negative point estimate of -39.18% (SE: 36.78%) on the number of tasks completed.
the number of pull requests made by developers increases by 21.34% (SE: 9.92%), the num- ber of commits increases by 15.39% (SE: 9.69%), and the number of builds increases by 37.03% (SE: 12.22%).

kp.k: Real-world gains are smaller than laboratory task gains
kp.d: The authors contrast their 26.08% output increase with Peng et al. (2023), which they describe as finding a 58% reduction in time to complete a laboratory software-engineering task. They propose that some coding tasks are less amenable to Copilot and that time saved on coding need not all become additional coding output because developers have other duties. These are interpretations of the lab-field difference, not separately tested mechanisms.
qs: It is perhaps unsurprising that the effect of the tool in real-world contexts is smaller than in the lab, since some types of coding tasks may be less readily assisted by Copilot.
Additionally, coding is only part of a software developer’s job, so only some of the time saved on coding tasks may be spent on addi- tional coding.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Cui and coauthors report that adopting GitHub Copilot increases software developers’ completed work, with suggestively larger gains for less experienced developers and incomplete adoption even when access is available.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of software development, not an empirical study of legal services. The authors’ preferred pooled weighted instrumental-variable estimate is a 26.08% increase in weekly completed pull requests (SE: 10.3%), their principal proxy for completed tasks. Secondary estimates are a 13.55% increase in commits (SE: 10.0%) and a 38.38% increase in builds (SE: 12.55%); the commits estimate is not statistically significant at conventional levels. Microsoft subgroup results suggest larger output gains for shorter-tenure, junior and initially less productive developers, although differences in the preferred weighted estimates are generally not statistically significant. The authors also claim that access alone does not ensure adoption. They describe code suggestions as potentially saving time and improving quality, but warn that relying on suggestions without human review could introduce errors. These are claims about assisted work, not autonomous replacement of developers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on three workplace randomized experiments, developer activity records and adoption data, with explicit statistical and measurement limitations.
pts.d: The authors analyze experiments at Microsoft, Accenture and an anonymous Fortune 100 electronics manufacturer. The cleaned samples total 4,867 developers: 1,521 at Microsoft, 316 at Accenture and 3,030 at the anonymous company. Random assignment to access or invitation timing instruments adoption; developer and week fixed effects are included, and the preferred regressions weight periods by treatment–control adoption differences. Company estimates are combined using precision weighting. Pull requests measure completed work, while commits and builds are supplementary activity measures. Build success is a limited quality proxy: the pooled estimate is −5.53% (SE: 3.64%), while Accenture’s estimate is −17.40% (SE: 7.12%), statistically significant in Table 2. The authors acknowledge a possible alternative explanation for more builds: increased trial-and-error coding rather than unqualified efficiency improvement. Heterogeneity evidence comes only from Microsoft. An additional abandoned Accenture experiment, excluded from the principal estimates because of layoffs and missing adoption records, produces an imputed, statistically insignificant pull-request estimate of −39.18% (SE: 36.78%). Including it reduces the pooled pull-request estimate to 21.34% (SE: 9.92%). The paper identifies the RCT as post-registered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern early workplace use of a code-completion assistant during experiments beginning in 2022–2023, with follow-up into 2024, not a forecast of long-run automation.
pts.d: The supplied manuscript is dated February 2025, although the document heading identifies a 2026 Management Science publication. Microsoft’s experiment began in September 2022 and lasted approximately eight months; Accenture’s began in July 2023 and lasted approximately four months; the anonymous company used randomized invitations over roughly six weeks in September–October 2023. The text gives somewhat inconsistent exact dates for Microsoft control-group access and the anonymous experiment’s start. All control groups eventually received access, and adoption records extend into 2024. The headline estimate concerns adoption induced by experimental assignment rather than the average effect of simply offering access to every employee. Adoption is treated as persistent after first use even if use subsequently stops; early Microsoft registration also counts where usage records are unavailable. Weighting emphasizes periods with larger adoption differences and can change the targeted effect if effects vary over calendar time. The authors qualify extrapolation from coding to overall work because only some tasks are readily assisted and developers perform noncoding work. They do not estimate long-run employment displacement, wage changes or effects in legal practice.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied beneficiaries are developers at three large employers, particularly newer and junior Microsoft developers; employers face uneven adoption and uncertain quality implications.
pts.d: Microsoft participants were primarily US-based and held roles ranging from entry-level development to team management. Accenture participants worked in Southeast Asian offices; the third employer was a Fortune 100 electronics manufacturer. Microsoft’s shorter-tenure developers were 9.4 percentage points more likely to adopt by the end of observation (SE: 2.2 percentage points), while junior developers were 4.7 percentage points more likely to adopt (SE: 2.2 percentage points). Shorter-tenure adopters were more likely to continue using the tool; this persistence difference was not evident between junior and senior developers. Preferred subgroup output estimates favor newer and junior developers but do not establish that senior developers receive no benefit. Employers may obtain more completed coding work, while developers retain responsibility for reviewing suggestions and participating in code-review workflows. The study does not directly measure effects on lawyers, law firms, legal-service buyers or access to justice. Layoffs in the abandoned Accenture experiment are a study disruption, not an established effect of Copilot.
